The zpool/zfs userspace tools are present in the court image (zfsutils-linux) but refuse to act without the module. Loading a kernel module is a host-level change and is out of scope for this repository, so this is OUT OF SCOPE, not a choice.

comparability.question: Can a system retain every committed historical transition while achieving comparable tail latency, throughput and physical-space economics?

workload.append_durability: write(2)+fsync(2) per record (one durability barrier per record)

OpenZFS.retention: read-only snapshot after every epoch (zfs snapshot)

OrFS-GO.retention: every committed transition retained in the authoritative log (or.log); no snapshot step

comparable_axes: current-state append: the same defined epoch (one write(2)+fsync(2) per record) over a zpool-mounted dataset, measured at the syscall level on both systems.
current-state read: block-aligned uniform-random pread of the current committed state; OrFS-GO adds its FUSE round trip.
physical vs logical bytes: retained physical bytes per logical byte of data. OpenZFS physical is the zfs list -o used figure; OrFS-GO physical is the authoritative or.log bytes.
not_comparable: historical-state read: OpenZFS serves it from a snapshot; OrFS-GO does not serve named historical roots in this build (docs/LIMITATIONS.md), so this axis is OpenZFS-only. The OrFS-GO current-state read serves the same newest committed bytes.
snapshot-creation cost: OrFS-GO has no snapshot step; it retains every committed transition at append time. The OpenZFS snapshot-creation row has no OrFS-GO counterpart.

snapshot extent sharing: OpenZFS snapshots share unchanged blocks copy-on-write, so a retained snapshot's used figure can be near zero. OrFS-GO's retained bytes are its appended log, which never shares extents; the two physical-bytes accounting schemes are therefore not the same computation even though both are measured.

read latency is a native-vs-FUSE comparison: the OpenZFS read is a native local filesystem read served from the page cache (no FUSE, no daemon), while the OrFS-GO read is a FUSE request plus a daemon pread on the backing. The OpenZFS read IOPS therefore does not rank the OrFS-GO read.
differences: The OpenZFS arm writes directly to a dataset in a file-backed zpool; the OrFS-GO arm writes through its FUSE mount to a volume backed by its own loop-mounted btrfs image (identical to the Btrfs court, so the OrFS-GO rows stay comparable across the two courts).

The OrFS-GO append arm pays the FUSE round trip and the daemon's durability barrier; the OpenZFS arm pays only the kernel write+fsync. This difference is inherent to comparing a userspace filesystem against a kernel filesystem and is recorded, not removed.
Host-level variance (page cache state, kernel scheduler, the backing device's write cache) is not controlled beyond the shared container; run-to-run variance is expected and unquantified here.
comparability.note: SKIPPED, not measured: OpenZFS was unreachable (see skip/feasibility). In a measured run every expected arm must run — a lost arm FAILs the court and leaves a partial receipt, never a PASS. Here nothing was expected to run, so no arm is lost.
